Geshur
GHEE-shur
proper noun / place
From Hebrew Geshur, a small Aramean kingdom east of the Sea of Galilee / Bashan fringe; home of Talmai and refuge of Absalom.

📖 Biblical Definition

Geshur is the petty kingdom of Talmai whose daughter Maacah became David’s wife and the mother of Absalom. The third son of David was Absalom the son of Maacah the daughter of Talmai king of Geshur. After Amnon’s sin and Absalom’s revenge, Absalom fled to Talmai in Geshur, and David mourned for his son every day. Three years Absalom remained in Geshur before Joab’s devices brought him home. The place is therefore written into the sorrow of David’s house. Political marriage to a border king could not purchase peace in the palace. Geshur received a fugitive prince and returned a polished rebel. Scripture does not romanticize the asylum. It shows how sin drives men across borders and how providence still holds the reins. Geshur stands as a reminder that foreign refuge is not final safety, and that the sins of a household will not be cured by geography. Only the God of David can heal the breach; Geshur can only host the wound for a season. The road to Geshur and the road home both ran through the unresolved justice of a father-king, and the later rebellion proved that time in a foreign court is no substitute for righteousness in Zion.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Aramean border kingdom of Talmai; maternal home of Absalom and his three-year refuge after killing Amnon.

expand to see more

GESHUR, a small Aramean kingdom east of Galilee’s waters.

Talmai king of Geshur was Absalom’s grandfather.

Absalom fled there after he slew Amnon.

David mourned while his son remained in Geshur three years.

The place hosts the bitter fruit of royal household sin.

📖 Key Scripture

2Sa 3:3 — "And his second, Chileab, of Abigail the wife of Nabal the Carmelite; and the third, Absalom the son of Maacah the daughter of Talmai king of Geshur;"

2Sa 13:37 — "But Absalom fled, and went to Talmai, the son of Ammihud, king of Geshur. And David mourned for his son every day."

2Sa 13:38 — "So Absalom fled, and went to Geshur, and was there three years."

2Sa 14:23 — "So Joab arose and went to Geshur, and brought Absalom to Jerusalem."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Geshur is more than a map pin; it is the foreign shelter where David’s unresolved justice festered into later rebellion.

expand to see more

The corruption is to treat Absalom’s flight as a mere dynastic episode without moral weight. Geshur becomes exotic background. Scripture instead presses the cost of delayed righteousness and partial love. David’s tears toward Geshur do not equal David’s obedience in Jerusalem. Modern sentimentality sides with the charming exile; the text sides with the holy God who will not be mocked in a king’s house.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. What must be recovered is the conviction that biblical geography is not scenery for myth, but the real theatre of the LORD’s providence, judgment, and grace. The places of Scripture stand as witnesses that God acts in history, among real peoples, on real soil, for the glory of His name.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Geshur is Talmai’s Aramean realm, woven into David’s marriage alliance and Absalom’s exile.

expand to see more

Hebrew — Geshur, Aramean border kingdom.

King — Talmai, father of Maacah.

Marriage — David’s union with Maacah.

Exile — Absalom flees there three years.

Lesson — foreign shelter cannot cleanse domestic sin.

Usage

"Absalom was the son of Maacah, daughter of Talmai king of Geshur."

"Absalom fled to Geshur after he killed Amnon."

"David mourned for his son while Geshur held him."
